hn-50597612.t: 87% of the Anthropic power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028
hn-50597612.s: A case study of Anthropic’s total power use and emissions. We find the company could emit 32 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2028.
ex: A case study of Anthropic’s total power use and emissions. We find the company could emit 32 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2028. In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”, we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032. But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers.

hn-50601525.s: How perplexity measures progress in AI models, and why it could help developers establish a shared approach to evaluating emerging capabilities.
ex: From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently⁠(opens in a new window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1 I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI.

hn-50599762.t: I built a game where you are an LLM's subagent
hn-50599762.s: A browser game where an AI manager thinks you are its subagent. Play at worker755.com
ex: A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/279ed2c4-59de-4d32-ad71-c5ee943adefe The manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator. It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review. Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds something new to lose.

hn-50603845.t: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
hn-50603845.s: We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it.
ex: We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it. With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle. OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience. That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI: a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.

ex: Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld. We have been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them. These findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. The results of this testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers. A live list of the security announcements we have received from providers is below. As the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers, we take data policy enforcement very seriously. We have taken the following actions: We are grateful for the Dragos report. As we integrate similar testing techniques into OpenRouter, we will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it. Not all affected providers have posted publicly.

hn-50596664.s: The Riemann Handbook: the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis in tamnd/riemann-lean, written as mathematics, as PDF and EPUB
ex: A book, in PDF and EPUB, that writes the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis in tamnd/riemann-lean as mathematics: definitions, theorems, lemmas and their proofs, in words. The claim is not checked. Nobody has built the Lean project in full yet, and no person has checked the written statements against the Lean code. This book explains the Lean code. It is not a separate check of the mathematics. See What is checked. Each declaration of the proof is inside the dominated subtree of exactly one other declaration (its immediate dominator, in the graph of uses from riemannHypothesis). The ledger gives an entry to each declaration whose dominated subtree is large, in tiers: 1,000 or more declarations (591 entries), 300 or more (1,927), 100 or more (5,764). It assigns each entry to a volume by its branch of the proof or by its Lean folder, and to a chapter by its Lean folder. In a chapter, the entries come from the top of the proof down. ledger/coverage.md has the numbers.

hn-50592097.s: A use-after-free in Ghostscript’s Type 1 font loader lets a crafted document cross Ghostscript’s -dSAFER sandbox, alter native path controls, and execute attacker-chosen commands as the rendering…
ex: A use-after-free in Ghostscript’s Type 1 font loader lets a crafted document cross Ghostscript’s -dSAFER sandbox, alter native path controls, and execute attacker-chosen commands as the rendering process. Ghostscript sits beneath print, email, upload, and preview workflows. Our ImageMagick research showed how files named .png or .jpg can still reach Ghostscript through image conversion. The index below records confirmed affected paths alongside additional applications whose renderer routes we traced. From the first escape to the downstream reports, fixes, and publication. The times on 17–18 September mark when the vendor reports were sent. Technical evidence and access conditions are in the index and writeup. Dropbox and the redacted services belong to separate Ghostscript findings. A single interpreter surfaced behind very different file-processing features. Each entry shows who can supply the file, where it goes, and what we observed or traced.

hn-50596133.t: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
hn-50596133.s: Japan’s automakers will work together to lower production costs as they band together to compete against China’s growing automotive sector.
ex: Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week. In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.

hn-50602843.t: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
hn-50602843.s: From Roseate Spoonbills in the Grassrivers to gulls over Vice Beach, here's what it takes to find Leonida’s birds, how the spotting mechanics work, and what Rockstar’s artists got right.
ex: I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching. A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than $1.8 billion in revenue the day it was released. Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy. But GTA 6 has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife.

hn-50600511.s: How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing?
ex: How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing? A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email. Whether your address is hosted by Proton, Posteo, Gmail or GMX, your digital letters reach their destination. This is the idea we build on. The year is 2028. Thanks to smart investment and political foresight, the Open Social Web has achieved its breakthrough. More than 100 million people connect, communicate and experience the world of open social networks. No platform economy à la Meta, ByteDance, Alphabet and co., no stressful digital moves and no toxic design. It works just like email: whether on Mastodon, Eurosky’s Mu or Streamplace, you have one account, your own posts and content, your own choices, and the freedom to connect with 100 million users worldwide.

gh-1466635339.s: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow: profile Python, Node or Ruby apps, port the hot functions with your coding agent, prove they behave the same.
ex: Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of target/. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway. fast-anything finds those functions, has your coding agent port only them to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible. Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain (rustup). --agent takes claude, codex, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand TASK.md to whatever you use. That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors.

gh-1467519193.s: make your macbook's trackpad talk using its haptic motor
ex: There's no speaker in a MacBook trackpad, just a small haptic motor that taps the glass so you feel a click. NO SPEAKER drives that motor up to 4,000 times a second, fast enough to make sound you can hear, and turns it into a voice. It talks, sings, raps, and becomes an instrument under your finger. One command. About a minute and a half. No speakers used. Downloads the latest release to ~/.local/bin/nospeaker and starts the show. a90.com/nospeaker points to play.sh in this repo, so you can read what it runs first. Grab nospeaker.zip from the latest release, unzip it and run ./nospeaker in Terminal. Signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple. Needs Xcode or the Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install). Builds one program for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs. A Force Touch trackpad (built into MacBooks from 2015 on, or a Magic Trackpad 2 or newer), and macOS 12 or later on Apple Silicon, or macOS 13 or later on Intel. Without a Force Touch trackpad, it says so and exits.
